title: Three perfect days in London
dek: The Lord Mayor's Show takes over the City, the London Jazz Festival opens, and two V&A exhibitions close. Here's a dry, cold weekend on both banks of the Thames and in the East End.

hero.caption: St Paul's Cathedral. On Saturday the Lord Mayor's State Coach stops on its steps for a blessing, just after noon.

intro:
Three things line up this weekend. The **EFG London Jazz Festival** opens on Friday and runs for ten days, through 22 November, with concerts in halls, clubs and pubs all over town. On Saturday the City of London holds the **Lord Mayor's Show**. The new Lord Mayor rides a gilded coach from Mansion House to the Royal Courts of Justice and back, with bands, floats and thousands of marchers behind. It's free and it's been going for centuries. On Sunday two shows at the V&A close: *Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art* in South Kensington and *Inside Aardman: Wallace & Gromit and Friends* at Young V&A in Bethnal Green.

So the plan stays east of the West End. Friday is on Bankside: Frida Kahlo at Tate Modern, lunch at Borough Market, a galleried coaching inn, and the festival's opening gala at the Royal Festival Hall. Saturday is in the City for the procession, then Sir John Soane's house and supper at St. JOHN before a concert at the Barbican. Sunday is the East End: bagels on Brick Lane, Columbia Road's flower market, a pub roast on Hackney Road and a free jazz broadcast at the Barbican.

The forecast early in the week is dry and cold, with highs of 8–9°C and lows near freezing, possibly fog on Saturday morning and a chance of showers on Sunday. The sun sets around 4:15 p.m., so do outdoor things early. The Christmas lights are already up across the West End. Bring gloves for the parade.

days.title: Friday: Bankside and the South Bank
days.intro: One stretch of the river, mostly indoors, ending at the jazz festival's opening night.

stops.name: Monmouth Coffee
stops.text: Start at the corner of Borough Market, where Monmouth has been roasting single-origin beans in nearby Bermondsey for years. Order a filter coffee, made one cone at a time, or a flat white, and buy a bag of beans for home. The shop opens at 7:30 a.m. Monday to Saturday and is closed on Sundays. Takeaway comes in reusable cups only, since it stopped using paper cups, so bring one or drink it there.

stops.name: Frida: The Making of an Icon at Tate Modern
stops.text: Tate Modern's big autumn show is about how Frida Kahlo became an icon: her paintings, her photographs and the image of her that spread around the world. It runs until 3 January, so it's busy at weekends. A Friday morning slot is the calmest time you'll get. Book a timed ticket ahead. Afterwards, the collection galleries and the view from the Blavatnik Building's top floor are free.

stops.name: Borough Market
stops.text: Walk ten minutes east along the river for lunch. On Fridays the market is open 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., and it's quieter than on Saturday. Graze rather than sit: oysters, a cheese toastie, a bowl of something hot from the stalls under the railway arches, and a doughnut to finish. Bring a bag if you want cheese or bread for the hotel room, and come hungry, since sampling is half the point.

stops.name: The George Inn
stops.text: London's last galleried coaching inn is down a cobbled yard off Borough High Street. The National Trust owns the building and Greene King runs the pub. Find a seat in one of the low, dark front rooms and have a pint and an early supper from the pub menu. Food is served from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m. On a Friday after work the yard fills with City drinkers, so arrive before five to get a table inside.

stops.name: The Thames Path to the South Bank
stops.text: Walk west along the river to the concert, about 30 minutes. You'll pass Southwark Cathedral, the Golden Hinde, Shakespeare's Globe and Tate Modern, with St Paul's lit up across the water from the Millennium Bridge. Then go under Blackfriars and Waterloo bridges to the Southbank Centre. It's dark by then and cold, but the path is lit and busy. If it's raining, take the Jubilee line from London Bridge to Waterloo instead. It's two stops.

stops.name: Jazz Voice at the Royal Festival Hall
stops.text: The festival always opens with Jazz Voice, a parade of singers each doing a song or two with a big band. Guy Barker arranges and conducts the EFG London Jazz Festival Orchestra, and Jumoké Fashola hosts. It runs about three hours, and tickets start at £42 plus a booking fee. The soloists hadn't been named when we checked, so treat it as a surprise.

days.title: Saturday: the City on parade
days.intro: The Square Mile closes to traffic for the Lord Mayor's Show. Watch it, then work west to Lincoln's Inn Fields and back to Smithfield.

stops.name: Duck & Waffle
stops.text: Duck & Waffle is on the 40th floor of Heron Tower and open 24 hours a day, so breakfast here comes with the whole City spread out below. If Saturday's fog has lifted, you can see the procession route. The dish to order is the one it's named after: a confit duck leg and a fried duck egg on a waffle, with mustard maple syrup. Book a window table. From here it's a 20-minute walk to St Paul's.

stops.name: The Lord Mayor's Show
stops.text: The procession leaves Mansion House at 11:00. The front reaches St Paul's at about 11:13, and the State Coach stops there at about 12:11 for a blessing. Wander.london suggests getting to St Paul's by 10:45, or to Fleet Street, which is quieter, by 11:00. The whole thing takes about an hour and a quarter to pass any one spot. It's free, there are no seats, and Bank station is the busiest way in. Use Blackfriars, Mansion House or City Thameslink instead.

stops.name: Ye Olde Cheshire Cheese
stops.text: Once the coach has gone by, walk down Fleet Street to this Samuel Smith's pub. It was rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666, and it's a warren of dark panelled rooms, some below ground. Dr Johnson and Dickens drank here. Food runs from noon to 2:30 p.m., so it's simple pub lunches and cheap Sam Smith's beer, not a gastropub. By 1 p.m. the procession's return leg is down on the Embankment, so Fleet Street quietens down.

stops.name: Sir John Soane's Museum
stops.text: The architect of the Bank of England filled his own three houses with antiquities, casts, paintings and mirrors. One room holds Hogarth's *A Rake's Progress* on folding panels, and the basement has an Egyptian sarcophagus. It's free, and you don't need to book. It's open Wednesday to Sunday from 10 to 5, and last entry is usually 4:30. On a busy afternoon it may stop letting people in, so get here by mid-afternoon. It's a ten-minute walk from Fleet Street.

stops.name: St. JOHN
stops.text: Fergus Henderson's whitewashed former smokehouse beside Smithfield Market is the restaurant that made nose-to-tail eating famous. The menu changes daily, but roast bone marrow with parsley salad is almost always on it, and so is Welsh rarebit. Finish with Eccles cake and Lancashire cheese. Supper on Saturday starts at 6 p.m. Book the first sitting and allow about an hour, since the Barbican is a ten-minute walk away. It's closed for supper on Sundays.

stops.name: Asha Puthli: The Cosmic Voyager at the Barbican
stops.text: Asha Puthli is a Mumbai-born singer whose music spans avant-garde jazz, Indian raga and operatic training. Tonight is a one-off UK concert with her band and guests: Anoushka Shankar on sitar, Yazz Ahmed on trumpet and Sarathy Korwar on percussion. Tickets are £34 to £49, including fees, and the doors open at 7. Earlier, at 4:15 p.m., the free *Rotterdam Loves London* set on the Barbican FreeStage is worth catching if you're nearby.

days.title: Sunday: the East End
days.intro: Flowers, bagels and a last look at Wallace and Gromit, then a long pub lunch and supper in Shoreditch.

stops.name: Beigel Bake
stops.text: The bakery at the top of Brick Lane is open 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Order the salt beef beigel: hot beef carved at the counter, with sharp mustard and a pickle. If that's too much for breakfast, have smoked salmon and cream cheese. It's quick and cheap. There'll be a queue on a Sunday morning, but it moves fast. Eat standing on the pavement, or carry it the ten minutes north to Columbia Road.

stops.name: Columbia Road Flower Market
stops.text: Every Sunday from 8 a.m. until about 3 p.m., this short Victorian street is lined with stalls selling cut flowers, bulbs, winter greenery and potted plants. The traders shout prices that drop as the day goes on. Go early, before the crowds. Look into the 60-odd small shops behind the stalls too, and the courtyard off Ezra Street, where a cart sells hot chocolate on Sundays. Small bunches travel fine in a coat pocket.

stops.name: Inside Aardman at Young V&A
stops.text: Today is the last day of the V&A's show about the Bristol studio behind Wallace & Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, with the models and sets from the films. It's a 15-minute walk east from Columbia Road. Young V&A opens daily from 10:00 to 17:45, and the main museum is free. The exhibition is ticketed, so book ahead for the final day, which is bound to be busy with families.

stops.name: The Marksman
stops.text: Jon Rotherham and Tom Harris, both from St. JOHN, run this old East End boozer, which is one of the best places in London for a Sunday roast. The Nudge lists Norfolk chicken, saddleback pork shoulder or Hereford beef, served with roast potatoes in dripping and cauliflower cheese, though the meats change. On Sundays lunch is served from noon to 3:30 p.m. Book the upstairs dining room, or take your chances in the downstairs bar with a pint of Bethnal Blond.

stops.name: 'Round Midnight on the Barbican FreeStage
stops.text: BBC Radio 3's jazz show goes out live from the Barbican foyer, with Soweto Kinch presenting. It's free, and you don't need to book: turn up and find a spot by the stage. From Hackney Road, take a bus or a black cab south, which takes about 20 minutes. The Barbican listing says 3:30 p.m., but another listing has 3 p.m., so arrive early. Afterwards, the conservatory, an indoor garden in the same building, is worth a look if it's open.

stops.name: Brat
stops.text: Tomos Parry's Michelin-starred room above a Redchurch Street bar is the best way to end the weekend. Everything is cooked over wood. The restaurant is named after the turbot, an old word for it, and the whole wood-grilled turbot is the dish to order. Start with something from the bar menu, such as roasted oysters with seaweed. Brat is open every day, with dinner from 5 p.m. Book through the website, or try for a seat at the counter.

stay.name: The Ned
stay.text: This is Lutyens's 1924 banking hall at 27 Poultry, now a hotel with 250 rooms, nine restaurants and a cocktail bar in the old vault behind a 20-ton door. There's a pool on the roof and another in the basement. It sits right beside Mansion House, where the Lord Mayor's Show starts and finishes, so on Saturday the parade goes past the door. It's also a short walk to the Bank and Monument stations and across London Bridge to Borough.

stay.name: Andaz London Liverpool Street
stay.text: The Great Eastern Hotel opened beside Liverpool Street station in 1884. Behind the Victorian red-brick front there's a modern interior with a Japanese restaurant, Miyako, and a Masonic temple in the basement. For this plan the location is right: Brick Lane and Columbia Road are a walk away on Sunday, the City on Saturday, and the Elizabeth line runs straight to Heathrow.

stay.name: citizenM Tower of London
stay.text: The rooms are compact and tech-heavy: an XL king bed, a rain shower, and a tablet that runs the lights and blinds. Some look out on Tower Bridge, the Gherkin and the Sky Garden. The cloudM bar on the ninth floor has the Tower and Tower Bridge below it, and canteenM serves food around the clock. Tower Hill station is about a minute away, and Borough Market is across the river.

events.name: EFG London Jazz Festival opens with Jazz Voice
events.text: The ten-day festival opens with its gala of singers and a big band, arranged and conducted by Guy Barker. Elsewhere on Friday, Morcheeba plays the Troxy.

events.name: Christmas at Kew opens
events.when: Fri., then nightly 4:20–10 p.m. to 3 Jan.
events.text: The light trail through Kew's gardens opens for the season. Tickets are timed, so book ahead.

events.name: The Lord Mayor's Show
events.where: Mansion House to the Royal Courts of Justice and back
events.text: The new Lord Mayor's procession goes past St Paul's and along Fleet Street, then returns along the Embankment. It's free. Most of the City is closed to traffic, Blackfriars Bridge is shut all day, and buses are diverted.

events.name: Goldie: Dare to Dream
events.text: The drum and bass pioneer plays a jazz festival show at the Southbank Centre. Earlier, from 12:30, there's free music by Tarana in the Clore Ballroom, including a 30-piece orchestra at 6:45 p.m.

events.name: Asha Puthli: The Cosmic Voyager
events.text: A one-off UK concert by the Mumbai-born singer, with Anoushka Shankar, Yazz Ahmed and Sarathy Korwar as guests.

events.name: Last day: Schiaparelli: Fashion Becomes Art
events.text: This is the V&A's survey of Elsa Schiaparelli, the surrealist couturier, and the first show of her work in the UK. Visit London lists weekend tickets at £30. Book a timed slot.

events.name: Last day: Inside Aardman: Wallace & Gromit and Friends
events.text: The Aardman exhibition closes after a nine-month run.

events.name: 'Round Midnight live with Soweto Kinch
events.text: A free live broadcast of BBC Radio 3's jazz programme from the Barbican foyer.

know: **From Heathrow (LHR):** the Elizabeth line runs east through Paddington, Tottenham Court Road and Farringdon to Liverpool Street, the station for the Andaz. It takes under an hour, and you pay with contactless. The Heathrow Express to Paddington takes about 15 minutes. A black cab takes about an hour. On Sunday the Elizabeth line is closed between Paddington and Liverpool Street until 10:15 a.m.

**From the other airports:** the Gatwick Express runs to Victoria, and Thameslink trains from Gatwick go straight to London Bridge and City Thameslink. The Stansted Express runs to Liverpool Street. London City is on the DLR, but on Sunday the DLR is closed between Tower Gateway and Shadwell, so change at Bank or Shadwell. From Luton, take the shuttle to Luton Airport Parkway, then a Thameslink train.
**Pay as you go:** tap a contactless card or phone at the gates when you go in and when you come out. Use the same card or phone all day, and the daily cap applies: £8.90 for zones 1–2.

**Northern line closures:** all weekend, the Northern line's Bank branch is closed during the day between Morden and Euston, and Battersea Power Station to Charing Cross is shut too. That means no Northern line trains at London Bridge, Borough or Bank on Saturday or Sunday. Use the Jubilee line, the District and Circle lines, or Thameslink. On Sunday the Hammersmith & City line is also closed between Plaistow and Barking from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m.

**Lord Mayor's Show day:** almost the whole City is closed to traffic on Saturday. Blackfriars Bridge is shut all day, and buses turn back at the City's edge. Walk, or use Farringdon, City Thameslink, Blackfriars, Mansion House or Cannon Street rather than Bank.
**Tipping:** many restaurants add a discretionary service charge, usually 12.5%. If it's on the bill, you don't need to tip again. In pubs you order and pay at the bar, and nobody expects a tip.

**Weather and light:** expect highs of about 8–9°C and lows near freezing, dry on Friday and Saturday, with a chance of showers on Sunday afternoon. Sunset is about 4:15 p.m. Wear layers and a warm coat for two hours of standing on Saturday.
